Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Bone is a living tissue. (i) Describe the three types of bone cells. (ii) Describe red and yellow bone marrow. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Bone cells: three types of cells are involved in the development, growth and remodelling of bones.
• Osteoblasts: bone-forming cells that synthesize and secrete unmineralized ground substance. Once surrounded by matrix, they become osteocytes.
• Osteocytes: mature bone cells lying in lacunae. They maintain healthy bone tissue by secreting enzymes and bone mineral content, and regulate the release of calcium from bone tissue to blood.
• Osteoclasts: develop from macrophages and carry out bone resorption, i.e. they break down bone and release calcium and phosphate in blood. Their work is important to the growth and repair of bone.

(ii) Bone marrow: many bones contain a soft tissue called bone marrow, red or yellow.
• Red bone marrow is found in spongy bone, the ends of long bones, ribs, vertebrae, the sternum and the pelvis. It produces red blood cells, platelets and white blood cells.
• Yellow bone marrow fills the shafts of long bones. It consists mostly of fat cells and serves as an energy reserve. When severe blood loss occurs it can be converted to red marrow and produce blood cells.

book_ref.quote: There are three types of cells i.e., osteoblasts, osteocytes, and osteoclasts

blocks.prompt: 2 Define osteogenesis. Describe how a long bone develops from cartilage, and how a few bones form without cartilage. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Osteogenesis: the process of bone formation. It begins during embryonic development and continues throughout life, playing a vital role in growth, maintenance and repair of bones. It has two pathways.

1. Formation of long bones (e.g. femur, humerus) from cartilage:
• The centre of the cartilage begins to harden (calcify) and the chondrocytes in this area die, leaving cavities.
• Blood vessels penetrate these cavities and introduce osteoblasts and osteoclasts.
• Osteoblasts (bone-forming cells) build bone tissue, replacing the cartilage. The step by which cartilage is replaced by bone by deposition of minerals is ossification.
• Osteoclasts (bone-resorbing cells) break down the calcified cartilage, making room for more bone.
• As the bone matures, some osteoblasts are trapped in bone tissue and become osteocytes, which maintain the bone structure.
• This continues until all cartilage is changed to bone except some at the articular (joint) surfaces.

2. Direct formation: a few bones, e.g. some bones of the skull, develop directly into hard bone without forming cartilage first. The cells are first scattered randomly in the embryonic connective tissue but soon fuse into layers and become flat plates of bone.

Even after bones are fully formed, osteogenesis continues as bone remodelling: osteoclasts break down old bone and osteoblasts form new bone.

book_ref.quote: The formation of long bones e.g., femur and humerus, involves the transition of cartilage into bone.

blocks.prompt: 3 Describe the structure of cartilage tissue. (i) Describe its perichondrium, matrix and cells. (ii) Compare bone and cartilage. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Structure of cartilage:
• Perichondrium: a layer of connective tissue surrounding the cartilage. It contains blood vessels, lymphatic vessels and nerves that supply the cartilage tissue.
• Cartilage matrix: inside the perichondrium; composed of collagen, elastin, proteoglycans and other fibres. It gives the tissue strength, flexibility and resistance to compression. Unlike other connective tissues, there are no blood vessels inside the matrix; the cells are supplied by diffusion, so cartilage heals very slowly.
• Chondrocytes: the cartilage cells, present in small spaces called lacunae embedded in the matrix. They synthesize and maintain the matrix.
Some cartilage remains throughout life to provide flexibility, e.g. between bones, end of the nose, outer ear and inside of the trachea.

(ii) Bone and cartilage are compared in the table.

blocks.prompt: 4 What is the axial skeleton? Describe the bones of the skull, middle ear and neck. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Axial skeleton: forms the axis of the body; its bones support and protect the organs of the head, neck and chest. It consists of the skull, ribs, spine and sternum.

Skull (22 bones):
• Cranium (brain box): eight cranial bones. Paired: parietal and temporal (2 pairs). Unpaired: frontal, occipital, ethmoid and sphenoid.
• Face: fourteen facial bones attached to the cranium. Paired (6 pairs): lacrimal, zygomatic, nasal, inferior nasal concha, maxilla and palatine. Unpaired: mandible (jaw bone) and vomer.

Middle ear: 6 bones (3 pairs) called ossicles: malleus, incus and stapes.

Neck bone: the hyoid, a small single bone at the base of the skull below the tongue. It does not articulate with any other bone of the head.

book_ref.quote: The axial skeleton forms the axis of the body.

blocks.prompt: 5 Describe the vertebral column and the rib cage of man. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Vertebral column: consists of 33 bones called vertebrae, in five groups:
• Seven cervical vertebrae: vertebrae of the neck; the first is the atlas and the second the axis.
• Twelve thoracic vertebrae: rib-carrying vertebrae of the chest region.
• Five lumbar vertebrae: in the abdominal region.
• Five sacral vertebrae: fused to form the sacrum, which articulates with the iliac bones of the hip to form the back of the pelvis.
• Four coccygeal vertebrae (coccyx): fused in adults. Sacral and coccygeal vertebrae together are the pelvic vertebrae.

Rib cage: 24 bones (12 pairs) called ribs and a sternum.
• Sternum (chest bone): a long flat bone in the central part of the chest.
• The ribs articulate posteriorly with the thoracic vertebrae.
• True ribs: the first 7 pairs, attached directly to the sternum by separate costal cartilages.
• False ribs: the 8th, 9th and 10th pairs, attached to the sternum by a common costal cartilage.
• Floating ribs: the last 2 pairs (11th and 12th), which do not attach to the sternum.

book_ref.quote: It consists of 33 bones called vertebrae.

blocks.prompt: 6 What is the appendicular skeleton? Describe the pectoral girdle and the pelvic girdle. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Appendicular skeleton: the bones present in the appendages (arms and legs): pectoral girdle, pelvic girdle, forelimbs and hindlimbs.

Pectoral girdle: 2 pairs of bones, a pair of clavicles (collar bones) and a pair of scapulae (shoulder bones). One end of each clavicle articulates with the sternum, the other end with the scapula. The spherical head of the humerus fits into the glenoid cavity.

Pelvic girdle: made of two hip bones. Each hip bone contains 3 bones: ilium, ischium and pubis. In each hip bone there is a bony socket, the acetabulum, formed by the fusion of these three bones; the head of the femur fits into it. The two hip bones are joined at the front by the pubic symphysis, a cartilaginous joint connecting the pubic bones at the midline. At the back the sacrum articulates with the iliac bones.

book_ref.quote: These are pectoral girdle, pelvic girdle, forelimbs and hindlimbs.

blocks.prompt: 7 Compare the bones of a forelimb with those of a hindlimb. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Each forelimb (arm, wrist, hand, fingers) and each hindlimb (leg, ankle, foot, toes) has 30 bones. The bones correspond as shown in the table.

Notes: the head of the humerus fits into the glenoid cavity, and the head of the femur into the acetabulum. Ulna is on the inner side and slightly bigger than radius, which is on the thumb side; the upper row of carpals articulates with the radius to form the wrist joint. The patella is embedded in a long tendon running over the knee joint. The fibula joins the tibia just below the knee and just above the ankle.

book_ref.quote: Each hindlimb (leg, ankle, foot, toes) consists of 30 bones.

blocks.prompt: 9 Describe the structure of a synovial joint and its six main types with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Synovial joints are the most common joints in the body and allow a wide range of movement.

Structure:
• Articular cartilage: smooth, tough, elastic hyaline cartilage covering the ends of the bones; it gives a smooth, frictionless surface for movement.
• Fibrous capsule: surrounds the joint and helps hold the bones together. It has an outer layer of ligaments and an inner lining of synovial membrane.
• Synovial membrane secretes synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint.
• Ligaments: strong bands of connective tissue connecting the bones in the joint.

Types (by range of motion):
1. Ball-and-socket: motion in all directions, e.g. shoulder and hip joints.
2. Hinge: movement in only one plane like a door hinge, e.g. elbow and knee.
3. Pivot: rotation around a single axis, e.g. between the first and second neck vertebrae.
4. Ellipsoidal: movement in two planes but not rotation, e.g. wrist with radius.
5. Saddle: movement in two planes because one bone is concave and the other convex, e.g. thumb joint.
6. Gliding: gliding movements, e.g. between the vertebrae and between the bones in wrist and ankle.

book_ref.quote: Synovial joints are the most common type of joint in the human body

blocks.prompt: 10 What is joint transplantation? Describe its four common types. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Joint transplantation is a surgical procedure in which a damaged joint is replaced with a healthy natural joint (from a donor) or an artificial joint. Common types:

1. Total joint replacement: the entire damaged joint is replaced with an artificial joint made of metal, plastic or ceramic.
2. Partial joint replacement: only the damaged part of the joint is replaced with an artificial component; often used in the knee joint.
3. Allograft transplantation: a healthy joint from a donor is transplanted to replace the damaged joint; often used in the ankle and knee joints.
4. Chondrocyte implantation: chondrocytes from the patient's own joint are implanted into the damaged joint; often used in the knee joint.

blocks.prompt: 11 Explain how the human skeleton and musculature help in the bipedal posture. Name the problems caused by improper posture. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Features that support bipedal posture:
1. The vertebral column has a distinctive S-shaped curve that distributes weight evenly and maintains balance while standing and walking.
2. The pelvis is shorter and broader; it stabilizes the torso and supports the body's weight on two legs.
3. The femur is angled inward towards the knee joint, keeping the body's centre of mass over the feet for stability.
4. The buttock muscles are much larger; they stabilize the torso and propel the body forward in walking.
5. The calf muscles are well developed, giving power for walking and running.
6. The foot has a longitudinal arch that absorbs shock and distributes weight evenly across the foot.
7. The toes are shorter and less prehensile, so the foot works effectively as a lever in walking and running.

Problems due to improper posture: vertebral misalignment (back and neck pain, herniated discs), joint strain (pain and inflammation of neck, shoulders, hips and knees, possibly arthritis) and muscle imbalances (bones and joints pulled out of alignment).

book_ref.quote: The bipedal posture of humans is linked to skeleton and musculature in several ways.

blocks.prompt: 13 Sprain is a common injury to joints. (i) What is a sprain? (ii) Describe the first aid treatment for a dislocation and a sprain. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Sprain: an injury to the ligaments that connect bones in a joint. It happens when the joint is forced beyond its normal range of motion, so the ligaments stretch or tear. Commonly injured ligaments are in the ankle, knee and wrist. Sprains are usually treated with physical therapy, and dressing is done to immobilize the sprain and give support.

(ii) First aid for dislocation and sprain:
1. Immobilize the affected area: keep it still and do not attempt to re-align a dislocated joint; use a sling or splint to support the limb.
2. Apply ice: an ice pack or cold compress reduces swelling and pain.
3. Elevate the affected limb: in a dislocation, if possible, raise the limb to help reduce swelling.
4. Seek medical attention: call emergency medical services 1122 or take the person to hospital. A dislocated joint is put back in place (reduced) by a doctor.

book_ref.quote: This can happen when the joint is forced beyond its normal range of motion

blocks.prompt: 14 Describe the biochemistry of thick and thin myofilaments of skeletal muscle. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Myofibrils are made of two types of myofilaments: thick (myosin) and thin (actin).

Thick myofilaments:
• about 16 nm in diameter, made of many myosin proteins;
• each myosin protein has two intertwined polypeptide chains ending in a globular 'head';
• the myosin heads extend from the thick filament and connect to actin during contraction.

Thin myofilaments: 7-8 nm in diameter, made of three proteins:
1. Actin: the core is two twisted strands of actin.
2. Tropomyosin: two strands wrap about the actin core and stiffen it; in a relaxed fibre they block the myosin binding sites on actin.
3. Troponin: present at regular intervals on the thin filament and made of three polypeptides: one inhibitory, binding to actin; the second binds to tropomyosin to keep it in place; the third binds to calcium ions.

book_ref.quote: Thick myofilaments, about 16 nm in diameter, are made up of many myosin proteins.

blocks.prompt: 15 Describe the bands and lines of a sarcomere. Explain what happens to each of them during muscle contraction. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Bands and lines of a sarcomere:
• Z-lines: protein discs to which the thin actin filaments are attached; the part between two Z-lines is a sarcomere, the smallest unit of contraction.
• A-band: dark band created by the thick (myosin) filaments, where thin filaments overlap them.
• I-band: light band created by the thin (actin) filaments.
• H-band (H-zone): the lighter central region of the A-band where no overlap occurs.
• M line: a dark line that may be present at the centre of the H-band; it helps stabilize the thick filaments.

Changes during contraction:
• The thin filaments slide deeper into the A-band, so the H-band and I-band narrow; the H-zone disappears.
• The Z-lines come closer together, so the sarcomere shortens.
• The A-bands themselves do not shorten; adjacent A-bands are pulled closer together.
• This happens simultaneously in all sarcomeres, so the whole muscle shortens.

book_ref.quote: During muscle contraction, the thin filaments slide deeper into the A-band

blocks.prompt: 16 Explain the roles of calcium ions and ATP in the contraction of a skeletal muscle. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Role of calcium ions:
• In a relaxed muscle the binding sites on actin are blocked by tropomyosin, so myosin heads cannot bind.
• A nerve impulse makes the motor neuron release acetylcholine; the sarcolemma produces its own impulse, which travels to the T-tubules and then to the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).
• The SR releases calcium ions into the cytosol. Calcium binds to troponin, which shifts tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin.
• The exposed sites let myosin heads bind and form cross-bridges, so contraction starts.

Role of ATP:
• In the relaxed state the myosin heads have already hydrolysed ATP into ADP and Pi
• After cross-bridges form, the heads release ADP and Pi, change conformation and bend towards the sarcomere centre, pulling actin: the power stroke.
• A new ATP molecule binds to the myosin head and allows it to detach from actin. Splitting this ATP into ADP and Pi returns the head to its original conformation, so the cycle can repeat.
• After death no ATP is produced, so cross-bridges cannot break: rigor mortis. During exercise, when ATP is depleted, the muscle can no longer contract (fatigue).

book_ref.quote: These calcium ions bind to troponin, causing it to shift tropomyosin

blocks.prompt: 17 How are skeletal muscles attached to bones? Explain the antagonistic arrangement of muscles with reference to flexors and extensors. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Attachment: skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tough connective tissues called tendons, formed at the muscle's ends by its collagen and connective tissue. A muscle usually has two attachment points on different bones:
• Origin: the end attached to the bone that stays stationary during contraction.
• Insertion: the end attached to the bone that moves.
• Belly: the middle part of the muscle.

Antagonistic arrangement: muscles can only pull, so to move bones at a joint in two directions they work in pairs that produce opposing actions.
• When the flexor contracts it bends the bone at the joint, while the extensor is relaxed.
• When the opposing extensor contracts it straightens the bone, while the flexor is relaxed.
• The pull of the opposing muscle lengthens the relaxed muscle again.
Example (knee): the hamstrings (back of thigh) flex the lower leg and the quadriceps (front of thigh) extend it; when one contracts, the other relaxes.

book_ref.quote: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tough connective tissues called tendons.
